item.title: Harness Deep Dive — Building a Claude Code-Style Personal Finance Agent with Microsoft Agent…
item.content:encoded:
Harness Deep Dive — Building a Claude Code-Style Personal Finance Agent with Microsoft Agent Framework

Background

In this article, I want to share what I learned about agent harness by building a CLI-style stock-investment agent inspired by Claude Code, and use that project to break down the value and role of an agent harness.

This article uses the harness module in the Microsoft Agent Framework, but the harness techniques and concepts we cover are not limited to that framework. Our focus is on understanding what a harness means, what it does, and where it fits. With that understanding, you will not be locked into any single framework.

What Is an Agent Harness?

Why do we need an agent harness in the first place?

If your agent simply connects to a few external tools, completes one operation based on the user’s question, lets the LLM process the result, and returns it to the user, then honestly, a harness does not matter much for that kind of simple scenario.

But if you are building an agent that needs to compete with top-tier agents such as Claude Code and GitHub Copilot CLI, you should ask yourself: does your agent support the following capabilities?

  • Context window management: compress and summarize conversation history to improve token efficiency and agent behavior accuracy.
  • Plan and execute dual modes: switch between two modes based on task complexity. For complex tasks, plan first, allow human review, then execute; for simple tasks, execute directly.
  • Multi-step task decomposition: break a complex task and plan into smaller, manageable subtasks.
  • Todo task loop: place decomposed subtasks into a ToDo List and loop through them one by one.
  • File-based long-term memory: persist important information to files within a session-based memory system so context-window management does not cause memory loss; support exporting and importing session memory to lay the foundation for long-running tasks.
  • File read/write: record agent output in files.
  • Shell: as the gateway to the underlying operating system, shell access gives an agent open-ended capability — any task a human can accomplish by running programs, an agent can attempt as well.
  • Skill: provide domain how-tos and load them progressively on demand to improve efficiency.
  • Web search: supplement knowledge through web search, which is essential for deep-research agents and therefore a core harness capability.
  • Code generation and execution: calculation-heavy tasks are not ideal for LLMs, so generating and executing code — relying on deterministic computation — is another must-have harness capability for powerful agents.
  • Background concurrent tasks: for very complex work, running multiple background subagents without blocking the user is also important.
  • Human approval: powerful agent capabilities require human approval to keep the system safe and stable.

If you use powerful agents like Claude Code and GitHub Copilot CLI regularly, you have probably experienced most of the capabilities above in one way or another. They all fall under the harness umbrella. In the sections below, let's walk through them one by one and make them less mysterious.

Case Study

Here we use the Microsoft Agent Framework to build a personal finance agent that helps users with portfolio analysis, market research, stock lookup, and risk and valuation analysis. This case study uses personal finance as the demo scenario, but the harness capabilities shown here apply to any domain.

Harness in Microsoft Agent Framework

Microsoft Agent Framework is Microsoft's unified agent development framework, consolidating the earlier Semantic Kernel and AutoGen frameworks. It is the direction Microsoft will continue investing in, so it is worth paying attention to.

For harness design, Agent Framework takes a very developer-friendly approach. It provides a factory function:

create_harness_agent()

In the simplest case, you only need two parameters:

  • client: the client used to communicate with the LLM. Common options include OpenAIChatCompletionClient and FoundryChatClient. The latter is how you talk to models on Foundry, and it is the one we use in this article.
  • agent_instructions: the agent's system instructions.

That’s right — unless you have special requirements, this alone gives you an agent harness, because other capabilities are enabled by default. If you want to turn off a specific harness capability, pass the corresponding parameter to create_harness_agent. The naming convention is disable_<harness_feature>, for example disable_todo, disable_mode, disable_file_memory, disable_compaction, and so on.

Smart design, right?

Textual Terminal Host

To run the agent, we need to provide a host that handles interaction between the agent and the user. For this, Agent Framework offers a library called console, which provides a text user interface (TUI) similar to Claude Code and GitHub Copilot CLI.

Great — on top of this foundation, we can demo various harness capabilities.

Demo

Mode Switching

By default, a harness agent runs in plan mode. In our early demos, the questions were relatively simple, so there was no need for plan mode. You can switch to execute mode with the /mode execute command:

As shown below:

Web Search

We provided this harness with a custom tool function that hardcodes stock data for several companies. Questions such as "What is the current price of a given stock?" trigger that tool:

For questions that require external information — such as a company’s latest financial news — you need web search instead, as shown below:

How web search is executed depends on the LLM client you choose. In our case, we use FoundryChatClient, which automatically uses Bing Search.

Session Memory

For valuable information, we want to persist it to files. That requires File I/O. For example, I asked the agent to add several stocks to my watchlist file:

The corresponding file appears under the current session directory:

Session Memory Export and Import

As mentioned above, you can export and import session memory with the session-export and session-import commands:

Plan First, Then Execute

For more complex tasks — such as asking the agent to review the current watchlist and then recommend a few stocks — you need to plan first and then execute:

The screenshot above shows the plan the agent produced.

ToDo List

Complex tasks like the one above are broken into multiple steps and managed through a ToDo List. You can inspect current task progress and status with the /todos command:

File Access Permissions

By default, the harness grants read/write access to session memory files. If your agent also needs to read or write other files, you can use the file_access_store parameter to specify which directory is accessible.

File read and write operations also require authorization. You can configure permissions based on your needs, for example:

auto_approval_rules=[FileAccessProvider.read_only_tools_auto_approval_rule]

With this setting, read operations skip the manual approval step. In the task below, the agent reads my portfolio.csv file without requiring human review:

By contrast, a write operation still requires human approval:

Skill

Agent skill provides a way to progressively load domain best practices. In this case, we configured two skills for the finance agent: valuation and risk-scoring, covering valuation theory and risk-control best practices respectively.

For example, when I asked the agent to value a company, it first loaded the valuation skill on demand and then performed the analysis based on that skill's content:

Shell

As mentioned at the beginning, shell access is a double-edged sword. On one hand, it unlocks enormous capability; on the other, it introduces significant security risk.

Agent Framework mitigates shell access risk in two ways:

  • Confined working directory: every command is re-anchored to a fixed directory and cannot escape it.
  • Deny-list policy: obviously destructive commands are blocked before execution.

You can configure this as shown below:

_VAULT_DIR = _WORKING_DIR / "confirmations"
LocalShellTool(
    mode="persistent",
    workdir=str(_VAULT_DIR),
    confine_workdir=True,
    policy=ShellPolicy(
        denylist=[
            r"\brm\s+-rf\b",
            r"\bsudo\b",
            r":\(\)\s*\{",  # fork-bomb shape
            r"\bmkfs\b",
            r">\s*/dev/sd",
        ],
    ),
    timeout=15,
)

With this configuration in place, I asked the agent to clean up files in that directory, and it solved the task using shell commands:

Code Generation and Execution

For tasks that require mathematical computation, we should dynamically generate and execute code. For example, the task below asks the agent to calculate the total value of my investment portfolio.

agent-framework uses the pydantic-monty Python interpreter for this. Pass it to the factory function as a context_provider:

agent = create_harness_agent(
    context_providers=[MontyCodeActProvider(approval_mode="always_require")],
)

Background Tasks

Agent Framework supports handing multiple tasks to background subagents concurrently and then aggregating the results.

In this case study, we wrapped the web-search-based stock research workflow into a subagent:

def _build_research_agent(client: FoundryChatClient) -> Any:
    """Build the lean, web-search-only chat agent used for per-ticker research."""
    return Agent(
        client=client,
        name="TickerResearchAgent",
        description="Searches the web for recent news and commentary about a single stock ticker.",
        tools=[client.get_web_search_tool()],
        instructions=(
            "You research a single stock ticker. Use the web search tool to find the most recent, "
            "relevant news and commentary, then return a short, factual summary (3-4 bullet points) "
            "with no preamble."
        ),
    )

Then pass it to the factory function as a background agent:

research_agent = _build_research_agent(client)

agent = create_harness_agent(
    background_agents=[research_agent],
)

This lets the agent search multiple tickers in parallel and produce a summary analysis:

Summary

By this point, you should have a clearer picture of what an agent harness actually is. It is not a single feature module, but a full runtime environment built around the LLM. If we think of an agent as Model + Harness, the model handles understanding and reasoning, while the harness makes the agent able to plan, remember, call tools, and execute safely.

In this article, we used a Claude Code–style personal finance agent to turn harness capabilities that often sound abstract into demos you can actually run and observe:

  • Task orchestration: mode switching, plan-then-execute, ToDo List, background subagents — this layer answers how complex tasks are broken down, executed, and kept from blocking the user.
  • Memory and persistence: Session Memory and its export/import — this layer answers how information survives across turns and across sessions.
  • Tools and capabilities: web search, Skill, code generation and execution, Shell — this layer answers how the agent gets external information, domain knowledge, deterministic computation, and system-level operations.
  • Safety and governance: file access permissions, human approval, Shell confinement and deny-list — this layer answers how stronger capabilities are paired with stronger boundaries and safety controls.

The value of Microsoft Agent Framework is that it packages these capabilities by default through create_harness_agent(). You do not have to assemble everything from scratch. Provide a client and agent_instructions, and you get a fully featured harness agent. When you need to trim capabilities, use disable_<feature> to turn them off selectively. That “batteries included, disable as needed” design lowers the barrier to building a top-tier agent experience.

One final point: this article uses personal finance as the demo scenario, but harness capabilities are domain-agnostic. Whether you are building a coding assistant, an ops agent, a research agent, or an enterprise knowledge assistant, the same capability stack applies. Once you understand what a harness is and where its boundaries lie, you are not locked into any one framework — knowing which capabilities you need matters more than memorizing a specific API surface.

I am Chris Bao, a Microsoft Certified Trainer focused on the Azure AI platform. I specialize in Azure AI services and agent development, and I provide training and consulting for organizations and individuals.

For collaboration, please contact: baoqger@gmail.com

item.title: Fabric: The Hidden Destination
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft Fabric is often treated as the end of the data pipeline, which becomes a problem when operational systems need those same events in real time. Azure workloads can subscribe to Fabric events in near real time once you add the EventStream destination many implementations overlook: a custom endpoint.

In this article, I’ll show you how to set up Fabric as an event source for Azure services. We’ll look at where the default configuration reaches its limits, why a unified namespace helps keep routing manageable, and how you can forward Fabric events to Azure workloads-all without creating duplicate ingestion paths or query jobs.

Microsoft Fabric overview

Fabric is the all-in-one analytics platform from Microsoft. Instead of combining Synapse, Data Factory, Stream Analytics, and Power BI yourself, you buy a capacity and get a set of workloads that all share the same storage layer.

Microsoft OneLake is a unified data lake for your whole organization. It’s a central repository where you can store, manage, and govern all your data for analytics and AI workloads across the organization. ( https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/fabric/onelake/onelake-overview)

Data Engineering, Data Factory, Data Warehouse, Databases, Real-Time Intelligence, and Power BI are all just solutions on top of that. The Fabric item you create in a workspace determines which experience you land in.

The Real-Time Intelligence workload offers you the following practical building blocks:

  • EventStream
    A pipeline that could transform events ingested by various sources and write them to one or more destinations.
  • Eventhouse A database designed for storing and analyzing streaming data , allowing update policies to transform data easily when ingested.
  • Activator
    An engine that watches a stream for conditions and triggers alerts, Power Automate flows, or Fabric jobs.
  • Real-Time Dashboard
    A dashboard enabling monitoring based on KQL queries against an Eventhouse without the need to create a full Power BI report.
  • Digital Twin Builder
    A Fabric component for mapping telemetry data and properties from multiple sources to twin instances in a graph of your physical assets and processes.

The Real-Time Hub builds the tenant-wide catalog of accessible streams anyone has published, so you can discover streams instead of manually looking for connection strings.

That stack is very good at getting data in. Ingest, transform, store, visualize, alert. The real payoff comes when you send the right events back out, so the operational side can act on Fabric output in near real time.

The weakness in integration

Making an Azure-hosted application respond to events produced by a Fabric EventStream can be tricky. The typical architecture looks like this, and the gap is obvious: it moves data into Fabric well, but leaves operational systems without a direct event source.

Everything from the sources flows nicely into the analytical world. The operational world in the diagram — an Azure Function reacting to a single event, a Logic App running a workflow, a service in Container Apps or AKS updating its own state — is built to react to events. But by default none of them has anything to subscribe to. The destinations people reach for first — Eventhouse, Lakehouse, Activator — don’t hand events off to Azure core services.

Fabric can emit events, but most people never look past the destination side of an EventStream. The payoff of going further is that Fabric no longer remains an analytical island. It can feed Azure services in near real time, allowing operational systems to react without extra ingestion paths.

The case for a Unified Namespace

If you’ve worked in the industrial IoT space before, you’ve probably come across the Unified Namespace (UNS). In a UNS, each system publishes states and events in a single, shared, structured namespace. In practice, this is usually an MQTT topic hierarchy like this:

Tags are published via the hierarchical path and can be subscribed to at whatever level of the hierarchy is required for the use-case. Point-to-point integrations can be avoided. A UNS gives you three properties that are exactly what this system needs. A routing key like enterprise/site/area/line/tag that contains asset identity and location. You can map it directly to an Event Grid subject and let subscribers filter by prefix without first parsing the payload. The second pillar is self-describing events, so analytical and operational consumers read the same fields. Fabric becomes one subscriber among many, not the central system every other app has to query.

If you’re building this system from scratch, model the UNS first and treat Fabric as a consumer of the UNS. If your events already arrive in Fabric in another format, the mapping described below still works. You’ll have to describe the routing key yourself.

One shortcut worth knowing about
You don’t have to bring your own broker. Event Grid’s own MQTT broker — a namespace with MQTT enabled — can be the UNS itself. EventStream has a native Azure Event Grid Namespace source that ingests MQTT telemetry and CloudEvents directly. This avoids the need for a custom endpoint and a Function App for ingress. Event Grid routing can push the same messages directly to a topic for operational consumers, without a Fabric round-trip.
That shortcut only ever relays what a producer already published, though. It has no opinion on anything Fabric itself produces, such as an Activator alert, an hourly average from a KQL query, or a Digital Twin Builder state change built from three streams and a lookup table. None of that exists as a message anywhere upstream, so there’s nothing for native MQTT routing to forward — it only runs on the ingress side of the pipe, before Fabric has done any work. Getting Fabric’s own output back out is the actual problem this article solves, and it’s the one leg no amount of broker choice removes.

Getting events out of an EventStream

An EventStream supports destinations such as Eventhouse, Lakehouse, Spark Notebook, derived stream, Activator, and the one we want: the custom endpoint. Microsoft describes it as the destination to use when you want to send live data to a system outside Microsoft Fabric.

When you add a custom endpoint destination and hit Publish, Fabric provisions an Event Hubs-compatible endpoint for you. In the Live View you select the destination tile and the Details pane shows protocol tabs (Event Hub, AMQP, and Kafka), each with a Basic page, a SAS Key Authentication page, and an Entra ID Authentication page.

The Event Hub tab presents a connection string in the format:

Endpoint=sb://eventstream-xxxxxxxx.servicebus.windows.net/;SharedAccessKeyName=key_xxxxxxxx;SharedAccessKey=xxxxxxxx;EntityPath=es_xxxxxxx

That’s a standard Event Hubs connection string, meaning clients that support Event Hubs will connect to your EventStream.

The Azure Functions Event Hubs trigger is one of them. For anything beyond a demo, use the Entra ID Authentication page instead of SAS keys, and grant your Function’s managed identity access, which saves you from having to rotate secrets later.

Why put an Azure Function in the middle?

A custom EventStream endpoint sends events via AMQP or Kafka. Messages are exchanged in batches using partitions and offsets. In contrast, Event Grid is based on messages with a type and a topic, utilizing its own filters, retry mechanisms, and dead-letter mechanisms. For this reason, a Function that acts as a translator between these two models is needed. It makes Fabric events usable for Event Grid and provides Azure services with an elegant way to process them in near real time.

It’s tempting to skip the Function and give every operational service its own consumer group on the custom endpoint. That solves fan-out — each consumer group gets an independent, full copy of the stream — but it doesn’t solve routing. Every consumer still receives every event on every partition; there’s no way to subscribe to just enterprise/site/area/line/* at the Event Hubs protocol level. Each service ends up parsing the entire stream, discarding most of it, maintaining its own checkpoint store, and requiring Entra ID access to the Fabric-side endpoint rather than a scoped Azure RBAC role on a topic.

This is what the MQTT shortcut can’t take over. A raw reading forwarded untouched is one thing — but an Activator alert or a KQL aggregate exists only because Fabric computed it. Getting either onto the custom endpoint means looping it back through an Activator action first. There’s no upstream message for native MQTT routing to relay instead.

An Azure Function responds to an event source via bindings instead of polling it. Via EventHubTrigger binding, the Function reads batches from the EventStream. The trigger is coupled with the EventGridOutput binding, which publishes translated events to the Event Grid topic. This allows Fabric events to flow to Azure services without querying.

Starting with the Fabric-to-Event-Grid function, the EventHubTrigger fires once per batch of events it reads off the EventStream. In the example below, it's wired up with a connection string, an entity name, and a consumer group. Add the Event Grid topic on the output side, and that's everything the Function needs to configure:

Connection on the EventGridOutput attribute selects identity-based auth, so there's no key in that setting. The Function's managed identity needs the EventGrid Data Sender role on the topic, same as the Entra ID route on the Event Hub side above.

One detail that costs people an afternoon:
Strip the EntityPath part out of the connection string. The Functions host wants the entity name in the trigger attribute, and a connection string that carries its own EntityPath will collide with it.

The EventStream trigger processes events in batches. From there, the Function maps the UNS topic to CloudEvent Subject and the last topic segment to CloudEvent Type.

Everything downstream uses the default Event Grid behavior, allowing a consumer to create its own subscription with filters, a retry policy, and a dead-letter target. Consumers don’t require Fabric workspace permissions.

As shown in the screenshots above, you define the source topic, the schema, the event type filter ( enterprise.uns.workplaceStatus), and the destination endpoint. Further, you can apply additional filters during subscription creation. For example, SubjectBeginsWith maps directly to your UNS prefix (for example, enterprise/demo/), so subscribers receive only events from the site scope they care about.

For the way back, the EventGridTrigger invokes the Function once per Event Grid event, and the EventHubOutput binding writes the result directly to the EventStream's ingestion endpoint.

This is half of the bridge the shortcut from earlier can replace: if your UNS already lives in an Event Grid namespace, point EventStream’s native Azure Event Grid Namespace source at it and skip this function entirely.

Important to know for implementation

If you are considering building a solution based on the described scenario, there are some pitfalls to watch out for.

Delivery is at-least-once on both hops. The Event Hub trigger can replay a batch after a failure, and Event Grid retries on its own. The downstream handlers need to be idempotent.

Partition counts can change. Microsoft notes that a data client using custom endpoints might need updating when the EventStream’s partition count increases, and that’s much better to know now than to find out at three in the morning.

Event Grid bills per operation, so forwarding every raw sensor value straight through it charges you for events nobody consumes. Filter or aggregate within the EventStream first, and forward only the events that a business process actually reacts to.

Event Grid caps events at 1 MB, and the effective sweet spot is far below that, so send a reference to the Eventhouse row rather than the full document if your payloads are large.

Fabric capacity is consumed the whole time the EventStream runs. A custom endpoint destination is cheaper than a Lakehouse destination, but it still counts against your capacity.

The end-to-end path (UNS -> EventStream -> Custom Endpoint -> Function App -> Event Grid -> Subscriber) typically takes low single-digit seconds.

If you need milliseconds instead for events that don’t require anything Fabric computes, subscribe to the broker directly — the shortcut from earlier — and let Fabric keep its own copy for analytics.

Wrapping up

With a custom endpoint and two Azure Functions, Fabric becomes part of your event-driven architecture. Microsoft Fabric stores the analytics copy in Eventhouse, and operational services subscribe to the data via Event Grid using the filters they need. This allows any Azure workload to respond to manufacturing events within seconds.

The complete sample, including the Terraform template for the Event Grid topic and a small MQTT publisher that fills the EventStream with UNS-shaped test data, is available on GitHub: Example of how to build bidirectional messaging between Fabric and Event Grid.

Once you use the custom EventStream endpoint as a bridge back to Azure services, there is no longer a hidden destination, and Fabric is no longer an analytical dead end. If you implement this pattern in your environment, I’d be interested to hear which parts worked well and where you had to make adjustments.

References

  • What is Microsoft Fabric?
  • What is OneLake?
  • What is Real-Time Intelligence?
  • Microsoft Fabric EventStreams overview
  • Add and manage a destination in an EventStream
  • Add a custom endpoint destination to an EventStream
  • Configure settings for a Fabric EventStream
  • Azure Event Hubs trigger for Azure Functions
  • Azure Event Grid output binding for Azure Functions
  • Event filtering for Azure Event Grid
  • Overview of the MQTT broker feature in Azure Event Grid

item.title: Request Coalescing: Preventing Duplicate Work in High-Concurrency Systems
item.content:encoded:
Imagine an endpoint GET /users/123 that reads from a database. Everything is fine until 1,000 requests for the same user arrive at nearly the same instant — the cache entry for a hot key just expired, or a normally quiet account suddenly went viral. Without protection, the database does identical work 1,000 times:

Request 1    ──> DB ──> User 123
Request 2    ──> DB ──> User 123
...
Request 1000 ──> DB ──> User 123

If every request needs the same result, why not let them share a single in-progress operation? That is the idea behind request coalescing:

When multiple concurrent requests ask for the same resource, combine them into one in-progress operation and share its result with all callers.
A ──┐                          ┌──> A
B ──┼──> One DB request ──> Result ──> B
C ──┘                          └──> C

Simple in spirit, but a correct implementation has to answer: How do requests discover that a fetch is already underway? How do they wait for it? What happens on failure, timeout, or across multiple application instances? We’ll build it up step by step.

The In-Flight Registry

We need a place to track operations that are currently in progress. In Java:

ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<User>> inFlight;

The key identifies the resource ("user:123"); the value is the operation that will eventually produce the result. Crucially, this is not a cache of completed results — it holds work in progress.

A CompletableFuture is a promise: "I don't have the User yet, but I will." Because it's a handle to a pending result rather than the result itself, we can hand the same Future to many callers.

Coalescing in Action

The first request for user:123 finds an empty map and creates Future F1, which kicks off the DB call:

inFlight: "user:123" ──> F1 ──> DB

A second and third request arrive before the DB responds. They find F1 already present and simply share it — no new database calls:

A ──┐
B ──┼──> F1 ──> DB
C ──┘

The magic is doing the “check for an existing operation, or create one” step atomically. A naive version has a race:

if (!inFlight.containsKey(userId)) {          // two threads can both
    inFlight.put(userId, fetchUserFromDB(userId)); // pass this check
}

computeIfAbsent() gives us the atomic check-and-create we need instead.

The Complete Local Implementation

private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<User>> inFlight =
        new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

public CompletableFuture<User> getUser(String userId) {
    return inFlight.computeIfAbsent(userId, key -> {
        CompletableFuture<User> future = fetchUserFromDB(key);
        future.whenComplete((result, error) -> inFlight.remove(key, future));
        return future;
    });
}

Two lines carry the weight: computeIfAbsent() and whenComplete().

return future does not block. It hands back the pending Future immediately — like a restaurant ticket that represents food not yet ready. This is the opposite of future.get() or future.join(), which block the calling thread until the result arrives. Returning the Future (or chaining with thenApply(...)) lets the request wait logically for the result without a thread sitting idle — which is exactly why async matters under high concurrency.

whenComplete() registers a cleanup callback that runs once the Future finishes, whether it succeeds or fails:

future.whenComplete((result, error) -> inFlight.remove(key, future));

We remove the entry after completion, not before — the registry is meant to hold only live operations. Removing it immediately would be wrong, since the DB call is still running. On success, the entry clears so a later request can start fresh work; on failure, it also clears so the next caller can retry.

Failure, Timeout, and Cancellation

When the DB call fails, F1 completes exceptionally, all shared callers observe the failure, whenComplete() removes it, and the next request starts a clean attempt.

Timeouts hide a subtler trap. Suppose the caller times out at T=5 but the database keeps working:

T=0   App starts DB request #1
T=5   caller times out, entry removed
T=6   new request starts DB request #2
T=10  DB request #1 finally completes  ← duplicate work
The lesson:
A caller giving up is not the same as cancelling the underlying operation.

A production implementation must define cancellation semantics deliberately.

Retries compound the risk. If a coalesced operation covering 1,000 callers fails and all 1,000 retry at once, you’ve manufactured a thundering herd. Coalescing is therefore usually paired with bounded retries, exponential backoff with jitter, circuit breakers, and caching.

Coalescing vs. Caching

These are complementary, not competing:

  • Caching stores a completed result: "user:123" → User
  • Coalescing tracks an operation in progress: "user:123" → Future<User>

Together they defend against a cache stampede:

Request ──> check cache ──HIT──> return
               │
              MISS
               │
          check in-flight ──EXISTS──> join existing Future
               │
          NOT EXISTS
               │
          start DB op ──> store in cache ──> complete Future

One subtlety: coalesced callers all receive the result computed at a single moment. If the fetch starts and a caller joins four seconds later, that caller gets four-second-old data. Usually harmless, but worth reasoning about deliberately when freshness is critical. Relatedly, the registry key must capture everything that distinguishes the result — not just the ID, but any parameter, tenant, or auth scope that changes what gets returned. Coalescing requests that only look identical is a correctness bug.

When Coalescing Is the Wrong Tool

Coalescing is a win only for read-heavy, idempotent, cacheable operations where duplicate work is genuinely wasteful. It backfires elsewhere:

  • Writes and non-idempotent operations. Ten POST requests are usually ten distinct intents. Collapsing them into one silently drops nine.
  • Requests that differ per caller. If the result depends on who’s asking — permissions, tenant, feature flags — sharing one Future leaks one caller’s data to another. (This is the key-scope problem above, stated as a hard rule: if the output can differ, don’t coalesce.)
  • Cheap or rarely-contended operations. The registry, the callbacks, and the cleanup all cost something. If duplicate calls are rare or trivially cheap, coalescing adds complexity for no benefit.

The technique earns its keep specifically when identical, expensive reads pile up under concurrency — not as a default wrapper around everything.

Scaling Out: Why Local Coalescing Breaks

Most systems run several instances behind a load balancer, and each JVM has its own ConcurrentHashMap. Three requests for the same user landing on three instances produce three separate Futures — and three DB calls:

App-1: user:123 → F1 ──> DB
App-2: user:123 → F2 ──> DB
App-3: user:123 → F3 ──> DB

The coalescing benefit is gone across instances. To recover it we need shared coordination — but note the key constraint:

You cannot put a CompletableFuture in Redis. A Future is a JVM-local object.

So distributed coalescing coordinates who does the work, while each instance still uses local Futures for its own callers.

Coordination with Redis

A distributed lock is one approach. An instance tries an atomic set-if-absent with an expiry:

SET request-lock:user:123 <token> NX EX 5

NX creates the key only if absent; EX 5 expires it after five seconds. Whoever wins becomes the leader and performs the DB call; the others are followers who need to obtain the result. Two common ways to propagate it:

  • Store the result in Redis (user-result:123 → User), which followers then read.
  • Publish via Pub/Sub, notifying followers directly — but Pub/Sub messages aren’t durable, so a follower disconnected at publish time misses it. A fallback is required. Redis Streams offer durable delivery at the cost of added complexity.

The lock-TTL problem

If the lock’s TTL is shorter than the operation, it expires mid-flight and a second instance acquires it — two DB calls again:

App-1 holds lock (TTL 5s) ──> DB takes 10s
T=5  lock expires
     App-2 acquires lock ──> DB

Mitigations — longer TTLs, lock renewal/heartbeats, fencing tokens — each add complexity. The same TTL/expiry mechanism is also what lets the system recover if the leader crashes: the lock eventually expires and a follower takes over.

Coordination with ZooKeeper

ZooKeeper is purpose-built for distributed coordination (leader election, locks, membership, failure detection). A common pattern uses ephemeral sequential nodes:

/coalesce/user:123/
    request-00001  → Leader   (lowest sequence)
    request-00002  → Follower
    request-00003  → Follower

Because the nodes are ephemeral, if the leader’s session dies, ZooKeeper removes its node automatically and request-00002 becomes the new leader — clean failover without manual TTL tuning.

But ZooKeeper is the coordination layer, not the result-sharing layer. It decides who owns the work; the result still has to travel through a cache or messaging system.

Do You Even Need to Build This?

Usually not. The from-scratch version above is worth understanding because it shows what’s happening under the hood — but in production, prefer a maintained implementation:

  • Go: the standard golang.org/x/sync/singleflight package is the canonical implementation. Its very name is the concept: at most one flight of a given key at a time.
  • JVM: Caffeine’s LoadingCache coalesces concurrent misses automatically — a request for a key already being loaded waits on the in-progress load rather than starting its own. For most Java services this is the right answer, not a hand-rolled ConcurrentHashMap.

Whatever you use, add a metric for the coalesced-hit ratio (how many requests joined an existing operation versus started a new one). Without it you can’t tell whether coalescing is actually firing or silently doing nothing.

Prefer the Simplest Architecture

Reaching for a distributed lock on every request is usually the wrong instinct. Ask first whether you truly need distributed coalescing. Often this layered approach is enough:

Request ──> L1 local cache ──miss──> L2 Redis cache ──miss──>
        local request coalescing ──> Database

This gives fast local reads, a shared cache across instances, reduced DB traffic, and coalescing of concurrent misses — without a distributed lock in the hot path.

The Deeper Lesson

The local implementation is genuinely simple: ConcurrentHashMap + CompletableFuture + computeIfAbsent() + whenComplete(). The complexity lives in distribution, where you must reason about leader election, lock expiration, leader crashes, partitions, duplicate execution, result propagation, retries, cancellation, stale data, and thundering herds.

Distributed request coalescing isn’t only a concurrency problem — it’s a distributed coordination problem.

Mentally, the local version is a fan-in of callers onto one Future; the distributed version is a fan-out of instances onto a coordination layer that decides ownership and routes the result back.

The idea starts deceptively small — if ten requests need identical work, why do it ten times? Locally the answer is elegant. The moment the system spans machines, the question becomes: across many nodes, who does the work, how do the others find the result, and what happens when that node disappears? That’s where a small concurrency optimization becomes a genuinely interesting distributed-systems problem.

Request Coalescing: Preventing Duplicate Work in High-Concurrency Systems was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
